title: TA9-11318
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, his common-law spouse, XXXXX XXXXX (female claimant) and their child, XXXXX XXXXX (minor claimant), citizens of the Czech Republic, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the IRPA). The claimants' identities have been established through certified copies of the claimants' passports.2 The mother was appointed designated representative of the minor claimant.
The female and minor claimants' did not provide narratives in their own Personal Information Forms (PIFs), however incidents relating to them were included in the claimant's narrative.

The claimant alleges that, as a Roma in the Czech Republic, he was discriminated against, harassed and harmed simply because of his race. The discrimination was on many levels including employment, education, housing and in the general public. He states that he was attacked in 2008 by skinheads while he was waiting for a streetcar. He states that he went to the police to report the incident but the police only laughed at him and told him to go home and wash.

At the hearing, the claimant testified that he had problems with the police in the summer of 2000. He had just purchased a XXXXX jacket and some police accused him of stealing it so they took him to the police station. He alleges that the police started beating him and that he was so scared that he attempted to jump out of a window (first floor). The police "brushed against" him and he fell injuring his legs. The claimant testified that his best friend was also brought to the police station and was beaten also. When the claimant was released from the police station after three hours, he requested that the police call an ambulance, however they did not. Instead his friend carried him on his back and they called a taxi to take them home. The claimant testified that he had to undergo surgery on both of his XXXXX: one because the XXXXX was broken and the other because the XXXXX was damaged. When asked if the police charged him with stealing the jacket, he replied, "No, but that he was suing the police" with the assistance of a lawyer by the name of XXXXX. The lawsuit, which took place in 2001 or 2002, was successful however and the case was closed due to lack of evidence.

Incidents related to the female claimant included being traumatized as a child due to threats made by skinheads, being hit on the head by a schoolmate and derogatory remarks made by teachers in 2000, while attending high school. She left high school in 2001 because she was very depressed and eventually hospitalized when she would not eat or drink anything. In 2002, her brother was assaulted by four skinheads, which resulted in her psychiatrist prescribing sleeping pills and additional pills to calm her. The female claimant stated other examples where she was not permitted to enter a music club, or swimming pool. In XXXXX 2008, the claimant went shopping and left her little dog outside while she went into the store. When she came out she saw a large group surrounding her dog and a police car nearby. An angry man told her in foul language that she should not have a dog and calling her nasty names. A woman tried to grab her neck however a policeman got between them.
The Board finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
The claimants' identities have been established as per the certified true copies of their passports.3 DETERMINATIVE ISSUES
The determinative issue is state protection.

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The principles, enunciated hereafter, pertain to the case at hand and were accordingly applied. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.4

No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.5

Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection does not mean that the state on the whole fails to protect its citizens, unless those failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.6 Indeed, if a claimant believes the actions of some police officers are corrupt, the onus is on the claimant to approach other members of the security forces or the authorities.7

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.8 The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.9 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.10

While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration,11 the preponderance of recent Federal Court decisions has held that the test for a finding of state protection is whether the protection is adequate, rather than effective per se.12 A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken, and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.13

The Board must consider what steps the claimants took to seek state protection. The claimant testified that he reported the 2008 incident to police but they simply laughed at him. The claimant was asked what expectations he had of the police that they would try and resolve his complaint. The claimant testified he expected that they would try to investigate his complaint but they did nothing and would not even take a report. The claimant testified and in fact wanted a postponement of the hearing in order to have documents translated that dealt with the incident in 2000 when police accused him of stealing the jacket. I did not postpone the hearing for this purpose but rather asked the claimant to explain what the documents were. With the assistance of the interpreter, I found that all the documents were dated in 2000 and were identified as i) a police report from XXXXX, ii) legal documents (Crown Attorney) relating to the processing of his complaint, and iii) a document from city Hall regarding the Licensing Board. The claimant stated that he received these documents two weeks prior to the hearing and that he was trying to get his medical documents to show his injuries.

Given the claimant's testimony of what transpired, I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of statements he made regarding what had happened. It appears that with the assistance of a lawyer, the claimant attempted to sue the police. The case however was according to the claimant, unsuccessful because of lack of evidence. I am unable to find that the claimant was denied opportunity to take legal action against police who he alleges were responsible for the injuries to his XXXXX. In any event, the claimant remained in the Czech Republic for eight years after this incident, without further interaction with police until he tried to make a complaint about skinheads who had beat him while on the streetcar/subway. I have no reason to doubt the statements made by the claimant in his narrative, which he affirmed were accurate and truthful. I do not accept that it was proper that the police laughed at him, however unfortunately the documents do indicate that police at times are less than helpful or even at times racist. However, having said that, I find that it is difficult to expect that police would be able to launch an investigation about whomever it was that beat the claimant without adequate or sufficient evidence. In addition, I find that it would be unreasonable to expect in any society that all violent acts reported to police would result in prosecutions or convictions.

When questioned about whether she made a report to the police regarding her situation in XXXXX 2008, the female claimant testified that she tried to get the police at the scene, who came between her and the man and woman who tried to hurt her, to take a report but they did not. She testified that her mother and father went to the police to lay a charge against an unknown perpetrator because they had no other choice as the officers at the scene did not take down the man or woman's names. She indicated that her mother, a XXXXX XXXXX, insisted that the female claimant write down what had happened but that, as far as she knows, nothing has happened. The claimant testified that her mother filed this report with the police in XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. When asked if she followed up, the female stated that, "of course she did. We went personally two weeks after the report was filed on XXXXX XXXXX, 2008 but we were told just to wait."

When the female claimant was asked what she expected the police to do, she replied that she expected them to talk to her about it and that the man and woman would be punished because it is not normal for a person to be attacked for no reason, especially when police saw everything. When asked if she attempted to file a charge against the police who were there because they failed to take a report including the names of the persons involved, she replied "yes, but after all those things that happened to my family, I stopped believing that the police would help me because everything always ended up like this." When asked if she filed a report with a higher police authority to complain that police were not servicing her properly, she replied that her mother was pushing for this but she was not successful.

The claimant to provide more detail regarding her family's situation. She testified that her father was a XXXXX XXXXX and that he had been attacked by skinheads and severely beaten, supposedly in retaliation for when her brother was attacked in 2002. She explained that her father was attacked because the skinheads who attacked her brother were forced by the Court to pay money to a gypsy. Since her brother had been paid the money, her father started receiving calls in 2007 or 2008 demanding money. When these calls were reported to authorities, the family's telephone lines were tapped but, as soon as they were tapped, the phone calls stopped. In addition, the female claimant provided a document14 from a lawyer who represented her brother who had been attacked by four individuals in 2002 and also a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, which details that the four individuals had been found guilty of a racially-motivated attack, ordered to recompense the victim (her brother), written letters of apology and were given suspended sentences, the longest of which was XXXXX XXXXX years.

The female claimant's testimony indicated that her mother, father, sister, brother and his brother's girlfriend departed the Czech Republic the day after she did, which was XXXXX, 2009. She wanted her claim to be joined with that of her family but her first lawyer, Mr. XXXXX, told her that it was not possible. Consequently, their claims were heard but the female claimant testified that they have yet to receive a decision.

The claimants were questioned about their views on state protection in the Czech Republic. The claimants responded that they do not believe state protection is available to them because protection did not materialize before when "we needed protection." The claimants responded that they do not believe state protection is available to them because protection did not materialize before when "we needed protection."

I found the claimant's responses regarding the effectiveness of state protection were not persuasive. Firstly, because documentation and testimony regarding their particular circumstances and that of the female claimant's family indicated that the perpetrators who beat up her brother were sentenced. Although the family was not happy with the sentences meted out, I agree that it was horrible that her brother became a victim of racial prejudice; I am unable to find the brother was denied justice. I can accept that the female claimant feels that justice has not been served, especially since her father was attacked; however, I have insufficient evidence regarding the circumstances of her father's attack. I therefore find the claimants' views on state protection were largely unsubstantiated and inconsistent with the documentary evidence which is drawn from publically accessible documents and from credible nongovernment and government organizations.

I acknowledge that there is information in the documentation to indicate that there is widespread reporting of incidents of intolerance, discrimination and persecution of Romani individuals in the Czech Republic. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that the Czech Republic candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the treatment of minorities in that country, especially in the case of the Roma. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in the Czech Republic for Roma who are victims of crime, police abuse, discrimination or persecution, that the Czech Republic is making serious efforts to address these problems, and that the police and government officials are both willing and able to protect victims.

Documentary evidence indicates that the Czech Republic is a multiparty parliamentary democracy with a population of approximately 10.2 million. Legislative authority is vested in the bicameral parliament, consisting of a Chamber of Deputies and Senate.

The national police are responsible for enforcing the law and maintaining public order. While law enforcement bodies were generally effective, corruption remained a problem. The Interior Ministry oversees police actions and is responsible for investigating allegations of police misconduct.
The laws provide for the right to a fair trial, and the independent judiciary generally enforced this right. Defendants enjoy a presumption of innocence. And trials are public.

According to Amnesty International, Roma continued to suffer discrimination from public officials and private individuals in education, housing, health and employment. Localities with marginalized Romani communities became targets of far-right groups; public officials continued to use racist language against the Roma.

The IRB undertook a fact-finding mission to the Czech Republic from March 23-March 31, 2009. The aim of the mission was to address information gaps related to the situation and treatment of Czech Roma. The results of this mission indicated that 80,000 of the country's 200,000 to 250,000 Roma inhabit some 300 so-called "socially excluded localities". These localities are mainly populated by Roma that have limited access to formal employment, education and adequate housing. The claimants in this particular case have lived, been educated and worked in XXXXX.

Interlocutors referred to legislation that provide for state protection of Roma; in particular, anti-discrimination and hate-crime legislation. The Czech Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of national, racial or ethnic background, as do other pieces of legislation, including laws governing employment and education and the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms. The Security Police Department of the Ministry of the Interior and the Czech Helsinky Committee noted that Czech criminal law outlines a number of provisions defining hate crimes. EU accession has led to changes and has had a positive impact on Czech Roma.

The Ministry of the Interior is responsible for maintaining the National Police Force in the Czech Republic. National law enforcement officers are solely responsible for public security and criminal investigations. Municipal or local police are responsible for maintaining public order such as traffic safety but do not have the power to arrest or conduct investigations. The national police are divided geographically into 8 regional directorates and 86 district directorates, which are further subdivided into 620 police stations and the national police employ an estimated 47,4000 officers and 11,600 civilian personnel.

When asked about police protection measures against discrimination and racially motivated violence, governmental interlocutors pointed to Roma Police Assistants, Minority Liaison Officers, and the Ministry of the Interior's Anti-Extremism Strategy. In addition, the Ministry of the Interior's Strategy on Policing Minorities was passed on 9 April 2008 under Government Resolution No. 384. The main objectives of this strategy include training on policing minority communities, efforts to employ minorities into the police force, researching crime in socially excluded localities, as well as maintaining the MLO and RPA initiatives.

Governmental and NGO interlocutors varied in their assessment of police relations with Roma. However, e.g. in Brno, it was indicated that police are frequently called to the scene of a conflict only to be told that the situation has been resolved. Similarly, Diapa noted that Roma often refuse to cooperate in follow-up investigations to crimes they report, subsequently leading to cases being dropped. However, several NGO and academic interlocutors commented that the police generally have a negative view of Roma that sometimes includes discriminatory of disrespectful attitudes.

The Inter-Ministerial Commission for Romani Community Affairs continued to take an active role in resolving disputes between Romani communities and their non-Romani neighbours and promoted anti-discrimination initiatives in housing and education. The Agency for Social Inclusion in Roma Localities now operates in 15 communities. Police set up an information campaign to recruit minorities into the police force in Prague, Usti and Labem and Brno.15

The documentary evidence notes that "the judicial proceedings on racial crime have increased in recent years due to the efforts of NGO's."16 The Czech Ombudsman was created in 1999 and is known as the Public Defender of Rights. The Ombudsman investigates allegations of public sector mistreatment of Roma and may take corrective action or issue advice or recommendations. The Ombudsman has successfully intervened in areas such as housing but has yet to receive any formal complaints against the police.17 However, he has received unofficial reports from NGOs and individuals alleging that they were bullied by state police, however, he could not act in the absence of formal complaints. There are other government and non government agencies available to assist the Roma, including 400 Roma NGO's, the Czech Trade Inspectorate (to deal with unfair business practices or consumer discrimination), and the Social Inclusion Agency to address the social integration of the Roma into Czech society, including housing, health care, employment, social services and cohesion.18 These NGOs are active in providing a range of services and activities for Roma, including monitoring cases of private sector discrimination and bringing such cases to court, provide legal assistance, monitor and speak out against neo-Nazi groups.

Some NGO's submit that impunity exists for racially motivated attacks and that police responses my not be sufficient however, the preponderance of evidence indicates that the state is taking action against extremists and does not condone or assent to extremist actions. The female claimant's evidence regarding the apprehension and conviction of racially motivated youth in attacking her brother is evidence on this point. I was not persuaded that the state was not taking action in the circumstances of her brother.

The Czech Trade Inspectorate is a state agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade which inspects business operations to ensure that they comply with Czech law and it has the power to impose fines for any breach. The Czech Helsinki Committee is an NGO that monitors and reports on the human rights situation in the Czech Republic, as well as assists individuals with free legal counseling and litigation. DROM is a Brno-based NGO that carries out a wide range of activities in Romani communities, including social and legal services, child care, education and recreational activities. IQ Roma Servis is a Brno-based NGO that provides community and social field work, free counseling and legal services together with employment support for Roma clients in socially excluded localities. Other organizations include Socioklub, The Association of the Romanies in Moravia, Zvule Prava, the League of Human Rights etc.

The Agency for Social Inclusion in the Roma Localities continued its efforts in implementing a long-term integration plan for the Roma. The agency synchronizes and evaluates social integration efforts by ministries and municipalities. In one successful program, the Ministry of the Interior, the local government, the police force, and NGOs collaborated to provide improved housing, trained Romani mentors to ensure that Romani offenders complete probation to avoid incarceration, higher police assistance to prevent crime, provide inclusion training to teachers, offer debt education training to young girls, and ensure media coverage of successful Roma. This program was expanded to seven additional areas and encompassed 28 ongoing projects.19 The female claimant's mother according to the female claimant was a XXXXX XXXXX.

The documentary evidence indicates that there are numerous recourses available to Roma victims when police refuse to respond or respond inadequately to requests for state protection, and describes details procedures for filing a complaint against the police, such as making a report to the Inspection of the Police of the Czech Republic, an independent body under the Minister of the Interior; or citizens can also register "complaints about police inaction and non-serious offenses by police officers" with the Office of Internal Control, which is part of the Police of the Czech Republic or to the Office of Internal Inspection; or to the Ombudsman.20

Therefore, having reviewed the evidence in its entirety, I find that the claimants have not satisfied the burden by providing clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming if the claimants should need it.

Accordingly, I find that the claimants would not face a serious possibility of persecution, or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be subject personally to a risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.

Accordingly, all three claims are rejected.
